extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum designers, and learning researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing instruction and learning environments that honor situated cognition and cognitive apprenticeship; emphasizes authentic activity, social interaction, and enculturation to develop conceptual knowledge. Useful for teachers, teacher-educators, and educational researchers planning classroom practice or curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity in activity is paramount for learning; conceptual knowledge is produced by and structured by the activity in which it is developed and deployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning tasks that are authentic, embedded in real or community-relevant activity rather than abstract exercises. Use tasks whose environmental features and purposes give learners meaningful reasons to use and rework concepts (examples: Schoenfeld's problem bringing and Lampert's coin problems). Avoid isolating concepts from the activities that give them meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge is situated/indexical
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge 'indexes' the situation that produces it; like indexical propositions, knowledge depends on the situation for interpretation and cannot be fully understood out of context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve situational cues and context in instruction; be cautious when translating indexical terms into lengthy descriptions—descriptions can become opaque. Learning designs should maintain connections between concepts and the situations in which they arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indexical representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexical representations developed through engagement in a task increase efficiency when parts of the structuring environment remain invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose learners repeatedly to recurring environmental features so that indexical encodings become useful (e.g., routines, sequences of action). Recognize that some knowledge works best when tied to situated cues rather than abstracted verbal descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed cognition (environmental contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of cognition is widely distributed throughout the environment, both social and physical; the environment contributes importantly to indexical representations people form in activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design physical and social environments (tools, artifacts, roles, community practices) that participate in cognition—e.g., provide external representations, collaborative workspaces, and artifacts that embody task structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive apprenticeship (modeling, coaching, fading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive apprenticeship methods enculturate students into authentic practices through modeling, coaching, and fading—teachers model strategies in situ, support learners' attempts, then empower independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement apprenticeship sequences: model expert practice in authentic contexts, scaffold learners' performance, gradually reduce support as competence grows. Use situated examples so belief systems and problem-solving habits are developed through practice rather than declared by the teacher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with learners' implicit, community knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin teaching with a task embedded in a familiar activity to show students the legitimacy of their implicit knowledge and use it as scaffolding for new learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start lessons from students' everyday experiences or culturally shared knowledge (e.g., coin problems for multiplication). Use these familiar contexts to introduce problems and progressively abstract to standard algorithms or principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-generated solution paths and narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow students to create stories and generate their own solution paths; these activities make them conscious, creative members of the problem-solving community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage learners to decompose problems in multiple ways, invent story-based representations, and justify or refine procedures based on those narratives. Treat multiple decompositions as tools judged relative to the task, not as absolute rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate multiple kinds of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a composite understanding that includes intuitive knowledge, computational (algorithmic) knowledge, concrete (model) knowledge, and principled knowledge (underlying principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure instruction so students acquire and connect these knowledge types—e.g., move from intuitive strategies to concrete models to algorithms to principles—so algorithms have meaning in context rather than being rote procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose learners to the culture and practices of the domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching should let students see the authentic ways of thinking and the conceptual viewpoint of practitioners (the culture of the field), not just techniques or answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make teacher practice visible: work problems collaboratively with students, analyze solution strategies, explore alternative approaches, and emphasize how practitioners reason and validate results. Do not treat correct answers as the end of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote social interaction and collaborative learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Social interaction and collaboration are central to learning; knowledge is constructed, validated, and distributed through social interaction within a community of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use group-based activities that enable conversation, negotiation, and shared problem solving. Design tasks that require role differentiation, joint reflection, and collective sense-making. Ensure structures allow peripheral participation and circulation of narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate peripheral participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Newcomers learn craft and practice by legitimate peripheral participation—observing, participating peripherally, and gradually moving toward fuller participation in the community's practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create communities of practice in which novices can observe experts and more experienced peers, take on peripheral tasks, and progressively assume central roles. Provide opportunities for observation, storytelling, and low-risk participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narratives and 'war stories' to circulate distributed knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives and conversations (including 'war stories') are essential modes by which community knowledge, practice, and conventions circulate and are appropriated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow storytelling, case discussion, and anecdotal explanations in learning environments. Use narratives to make tacit practices explicit and to transmit contextualized problem-solving knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group learning affordances (collective problem solving and role-display)
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups support synergistic insights not available to individuals; groups also permit display of multiple roles needed for authentic tasks and foster reflective discussion about those roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that require coordinated roles (e.g., strategist, recorder, critic) and that provoke discussion about the aptness of those roles. Use group composition and tasks to surface diverse perspectives and support role learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confront misconceptions through collaborative elicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups can draw out, confront, and discuss students' ineffective strategies and deep misconceptions that individual assessment may miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use peer discussion, problem explanation, and collective sense-making to surface misconceptions. Teachers should listen for surface retellings vs genuine understanding and design activities that make underlying beliefs visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop collaborative work skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need situated opportunities to develop skills for collaborative work, since workplace and real-world problem solving is often collaborative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and scaffold collaboration explicitly through structured group tasks, norms for interaction, and reflection on group processes so students learn how to learn and work with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster articulation, reflection, and generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration leads to articulation or manifestation of strategies, which can be discussed and reflected on; such reflection fosters grounded generalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include activities that require learners to articulate their strategies, compare approaches, and reflect on effectiveness—use these reflective episodes as a bridge from situated practice to broader principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice in multiple authentic contexts for situated generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrent, authentic practice across multiple contexts produces densely textured, generalizable conceptual knowledge that is not abstract but situated across contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide repeated opportunities to apply ideas in varied, authentic contexts so learners develop flexible, context-rich understandings rather than decontextualized rule-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess heuristics and algorithms relative to tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics are not absolute; different decompositions and algorithms are more or less useful depending on the task and the problem solvers' interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to evaluate and choose among heuristics and algorithms based on task demands, efficiency, and community norms rather than presenting a single 'right' method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-explication; preserve implicit/contextual constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A difficult pedagogic challenge is separating what should be made explicit from what should remain implicit; excessive explication can lift implicit constraints out of the world and make them awkward objects of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about translating all tacit knowledge into explicit rules—some indexical/contextual cues should remain implicit to preserve efficiency and situated meaning. Seek an appropriate balance between explicit instruction and preserved context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunities to observe practitioners engaged in authentic practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners benefit from observing teachers and experts engaged in real practice; few students before graduate level see teachers doing the work they are expected to learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate live modeling, think-alouds, public problem solving, or apprenticeships that let learners watch authentic expert activity rather than simply receiving decontextualized instruction.
